note: Summaries written for this project. They paraphrase public guidance and are not quotations or legal advice.

cards.title: Professional nominee directors fronting many companies
cards.summary: A nominee director lends a name to companies that are run by someone else. The nominee satisfies the legal requirement for a natural person on the board while the real controller stays out of the public record.
indicators: One natural person holds an unusually large number of directorships
The companies behind those appointments are dormant, never file accounts or are dissolved within two years
The nominee is the only director of each company
The nominee lives in a different country from the stated business
Appointments cluster at a small number of shared addresses
cards.why: Volume on its own is not proof. Accountants and professional directors also hold many appointments. The combination of volume with disposable companies and sole directorships is what marks a nominee network.
actions: Request evidence of who gives instructions to the director
Treat every company fronted by the same nominee as one connected risk
Apply enhanced due diligence before onboarding or continuing the relationship
sources: FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)
HM Treasury and Home Office, National Risk Assessment of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (2020)

cards.title: Informal nominees and front persons
cards.summary: Controllers also use relatives, employees or paid strangers as the declared owner. These front persons appear as the person with significant control but have no means or expertise that would explain the holding.
indicators: The declared owner controls several unrelated companies in unrelated sectors
The declared owner has no visible business history
The declared owner and the director are both resident overseas
Control records are filed on the day of incorporation and never updated
cards.why: A front person makes the register look complete. The absence of a gap is exactly what hides the real controller.
actions: Ask for source of wealth evidence for the declared owner
Compare the declared owner with signatories and people who give payment instructions
Escalate where the declared owner cannot explain the business
sources: FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)
FATF, Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons (2023)

cards.title: Identity variation used to defeat counting
cards.summary: The same person can be filed under different spellings, with or without middle names, with initials, or with a slightly different month of birth. Each variation looks like a new individual to a system that counts exact names.
indicators: Several officer records share a surname, a month and year of birth and near identical forenames
Spelling differences are small and inconsistent across filings
The variations all lead to companies at the same addresses
cards.why: Counting appointments by exact name undercounts prolific nominees. Entity resolution on name and date of birth is needed before any volume rule is applied.
actions: Resolve officer identities before applying appointment thresholds
Use identity verification status from the registrar where it is available
Record every spelling variant in the case file
sources: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023
FATF, Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons (2023)

cards.title: Mass registration addresses and company factories
cards.summary: Some addresses host hundreds or thousands of companies that exist only on paper. They are created in batches, used briefly as vehicles for fraud or laundering, and abandoned.
indicators: A very large number of companies share one registered office
Most companies at the address are dissolved within two years or never file accounts
Directors are predominantly resident overseas
Incorporations arrive in waves within a few days of each other
A handful of directors account for most companies at the address
cards.why: A registered office gives a shell an appearance of UK substance. A shared address with a high share of disposable companies is one of the strongest network level indicators available from public data.
actions: Treat the address as a risk factor for every company registered there
Check whether the business has any real presence at the address
Report suspected false addresses to the registrar
sources: HM Treasury and Home Office, National Risk Assessment of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (2020)
FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)

cards.title: Distinguishing formation agents from company factories
cards.summary: Trust and company service providers, accountants and virtual offices legitimately host many companies. Their client companies live for years, file accounts on time and have diverse, mostly local directors.
indicators: Low share of early dissolutions at the address
Accounts filed on time by most companies
Many different directors, each with few companies
Incorporation dates spread evenly over time
cards.why: An address count alone produces large numbers of false alerts on legitimate agents. The behaviour of the companies at the address separates the two.
actions: Check that the service provider is supervised for anti money laundering purposes
Use address behaviour, not address volume, to set risk
Do not exit customers only because they use a shared office
sources: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group, Guidance for the UK Financial Sector

cards.title: Registered office abuse and inappropriate addresses
cards.summary: Companies have been registered at addresses without the knowledge of the occupier, or at addresses where documents cannot be delivered. Recent reforms require every company to keep an appropriate registered office address and give the registrar power to change it.
indicators: Residents or businesses at the address deny any link to the company
The address is a mail drop with no ability to acknowledge documents
The registrar has moved the company to a default address
cards.why: An inappropriate registered office is now itself a compliance failure and can lead to strike off.
actions: Verify the registered office independently
Check the filing history for address changes imposed by the registrar
sources: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023

cards.title: Circular ownership structures
cards.summary: In a circular structure each company is recorded as controlled by another company in the same group, and the chain eventually returns to where it started. No natural person appears at any point.
indicators: Company A lists company B as its controller while B, directly or through others, lists A
No individual person with significant control anywhere in the group
The same director sits on every company in the loop
cards.why: A loop of declared control cannot be a true statement of ultimate ownership. It either conceals the real owner or reflects false filings, and both justify escalation.
actions: Refuse to accept the structure as evidence of beneficial ownership
Require the customer to name the natural persons who ultimately benefit
Report the discrepancy to the registrar
sources: FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)
Companies Act 2006, Part 21A (persons with significant control)

cards.title: Cross border loops through offshore entities
cards.summary: A loop is harder to see when one link runs through an entity registered offshore. The UK register shows an overseas corporate controller, and only foreign or leaked records show that the overseas entity is in turn held by another UK company in the same group.
indicators: A corporate controller registered in a secrecy jurisdiction
Leak data names a UK company as shareholder of that offshore entity
The UK shareholder is itself controlled by the first company or its subsidiaries
cards.why: Each national register looks unremarkable in isolation. The loop only appears when the datasets are joined.
actions: Join domestic control records with overseas and leaked ownership data
Ask for certified registers of members for the offshore entity
sources: FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)
FATF, Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons (2023)

cards.title: Layering through long chains of corporate owners
cards.summary: Chains of several corporate owners placed one above another add distance between an asset and its owner. Each added layer raises the cost of tracing without any commercial purpose.
indicators: Three or more corporate layers above an operating company
Layers registered in different countries
Layers with no employees, premises or accounts
cards.why: Complexity without a commercial rationale is a recognised indicator of concealment.
actions: Ask for the commercial reason for each layer
Obtain a full structure chart signed by a senior officer
sources: FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group, Guidance for the UK Financial Sector

cards.title: Indirect ownership or control by designated persons
cards.summary: UK financial sanctions apply not only to a designated person but also to any entity that the person owns or controls, directly or indirectly. Ownership means holding more than 50 percent of the shares or voting rights or the right to appoint or remove a majority of the board. Control also exists where it is reasonable to expect that the person can ensure the affairs of the entity are conducted in line with their wishes.
indicators: A designated person is a person with significant control or director of the company
A designated person controls an entity that in turn controls the company
The chain between the designated person and the company is made of majority holdings
cards.why: An entity that is owned or controlled by a designated person is treated as subject to the same asset freeze even if it is not named on the list.
actions: Freeze and do not deal with funds where ownership or control is established
Report to OFSI as required
Seek legal advice where control is suspected but not established
sources: OFSI, UK Financial Sanctions General Guidance
Sanctions and Anti Money Laundering Act 2018

cards.title: Aggregation of holdings and the fifty percent rule
cards.summary: Under the United States rule, an entity owned 50 percent or more in aggregate by one or more blocked persons is itself blocked. UK guidance takes a different view of aggregation: holdings of different designated persons are not simply added together unless there is a joint arrangement or one controls the rights of the other.
indicators: Two or more listed parties each hold a minority stake
Minority stakes that together exceed half of the shares
Shareholders that act together under an agreement
cards.why: The same structure can be blocked under one regime and not under another, so exposure has to be assessed regime by regime.
actions: Compute effective ownership along every path from a listed party
Assess each applicable sanctions regime separately
sources: OFAC, Guidance on Entities Owned by Persons Whose Property Is Blocked (50 Percent Rule)
OFSI, UK Financial Sanctions General Guidance

cards.title: Name variants and transliteration in screening
cards.summary: Names written in other scripts can be rendered in the Latin alphabet in many ways. Lists publish some aliases, but a registry filing may use a spelling that is on no list.
indicators: A name differs from a list entry only by vowels, doubled letters or common letter substitutions
Surname and forename order is reversed
Date of birth agrees with the list entry
cards.why: Exact matching misses designated persons. Fuzzy matching without secondary identifiers produces unmanageable false alerts. Both name similarity and date of birth are needed.
actions: Screen with transliteration aware matching
Use date of birth and nationality to confirm or discount a name match
Record why each potential match was confirmed or discounted
sources: OFSI, UK Financial Sanctions General Guidance
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group, Guidance for the UK Financial Sector

cards.title: Handling name only matches
cards.summary: A match on name alone, with no date of birth or other identifier to confirm it, is a potential match and not a finding. Common names produce many such matches against innocent people.
indicators: The source record has no date of birth
The list entry has no date of birth
Year of birth agrees but month does not
cards.why: Acting on an unconfirmed match harms an innocent customer. Ignoring it risks a sanctions breach. The correct response is review by a trained person.
actions: Route name only matches to manual review
Seek additional identifiers before any adverse action
Do not describe a potential match as a confirmed designation
sources: OFSI, UK Financial Sanctions General Guidance
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group, Guidance for the UK Financial Sector

cards.title: Corporate controllers registered in secrecy jurisdictions
cards.summary: A company may record another legal entity as its person with significant control only when that entity is itself subject to equivalent disclosure, for example because it keeps its own control register or is listed on a qualifying market. A private company from a secrecy jurisdiction does not normally meet that test, so the filing should have looked through it to the individuals behind it.
indicators: The only registered controller is a corporate entity from a secrecy jurisdiction
The legal form given is an international business company or similar
No natural person appears anywhere in the declared chain
cards.why: Recording an offshore company as the controller ends the public trail at the border. It is one of the most common ways the control register is defeated.
actions: Require identification of the natural persons behind the offshore entity
Obtain certified ownership documents from the offshore registered agent
Report the discrepancy between the register and the information obtained
sources: Companies Act 2006, Part 21A (persons with significant control)
FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)
FATF, Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons (2023)

cards.title: Statements that there is no registrable person
cards.summary: A company can state that it has no person with significant control. That is true for companies with widely spread ownership, but the statement is also used to avoid naming a controller.
indicators: A small private company with one director states that nobody controls it
The statement is combined with corporate officers or overseas directors
cards.why: For a closely held company the statement is implausible and should be challenged.
actions: Obtain the register of members and compare holdings with the statement
Challenge the statement where a single shareholder holds more than a quarter
sources: Companies Act 2006, Part 21A (persons with significant control)
FATF, Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons (2023)

cards.title: Hidden controllers revealed by leak data
cards.summary: Leaked records from offshore service providers sometimes name the shareholders, directors or beneficiaries of an entity that the official register leaves blank. Joining those records to the control register can reveal a person behind an opaque chain.
indicators: An offshore controller has named officers in leak data
Those officers do not appear anywhere in the UK register for the company
cards.why: Leak data can close a gap in the declared chain. It is also dated, incomplete and unverified, and appearing in it is not evidence of wrongdoing since offshore entities have lawful uses.
actions: Treat leak data as a lead to verify, never as proof
Ask the customer to confirm or explain the relationship
Record the source and date of the leaked record
sources: ICIJ, Offshore Leaks Database notes on use of the data
FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)

cards.title: Legitimate foreign parent structures
cards.summary: Subsidiaries of listed or regulated foreign groups also show a corporate controller and no natural person. They differ from concealment structures because the parent is subject to public disclosure in its home market and the subsidiary files full accounts.
indicators: Parent is listed or regulated in a jurisdiction with public ownership disclosure
Subsidiary files audited or full accounts
Directors are employees of the group
cards.why: Treating every corporate controller as suspicious floods reviewers with alerts on ordinary multinational groups.
actions: Verify the listing or regulatory status of the parent
Apply standard rather than enhanced due diligence where the parent is transparent
sources: Companies Act 2006, Part 21A (persons with significant control)
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group, Guidance for the UK Financial Sector

cards.title: Phoenix companies
cards.summary: A phoenix company is created to carry on the business of a company that has been dissolved or has failed, with the same people behind it and a near identical name, leaving creditors and tax debts with the old company.
indicators: A new company is incorporated within weeks of the dissolution of a similarly named company
Same director and same address as the dissolved company
The dissolved company never filed accounts
The pattern repeats several times
cards.why: Reusing the name of a company that went into insolvent liquidation is restricted, and directors of dissolved companies can be investigated and disqualified.
actions: Review the history of dissolved companies linked to the director
Check for unpaid creditors and tax debts of the predecessor
Consider a report to the Insolvency Service
sources: Insolvency Act 1986, section 216
Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986

cards.title: Burst incorporation of shell batches
cards.summary: Batches of companies are formed on the same day or within a few days by the same person at the same address, used for a short campaign such as invoice fraud or mule accounts, and then left to be struck off.
indicators: Many companies incorporated within days by one director
Names that share a common stem
No accounts filed and dissolution within eighteen months
cards.why: A batch gives an offender a supply of fresh bank accounts and trading names that can be discarded as each one is detected.
actions: Link all members of the batch in one case
Check whether accounts opened for batch members show similar activity
sources: HM Treasury and Home Office, National Risk Assessment of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (2020)
FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)

cards.title: Legitimate batches such as property special purpose vehicles
cards.summary: Developers and investors lawfully create several companies at once, often one per property or project. These companies stay on the register for years and file accounts.
indicators: Batch members remain active for many years
Accounts are filed for each company
Directors are resident locally
cards.why: Same day incorporation is not suspicious by itself. Abandonment is what separates a disposable batch from a project structure.
actions: Confirm the commercial purpose of the batch
Apply standard due diligence where the companies show real activity
sources: Joint Money Laundering Steering Group, Guidance for the UK Financial Sector

cards.title: Customer due diligence on ownership and control
cards.summary: A regulated firm must identify the beneficial owner of a corporate customer, take reasonable measures to verify that identity and understand the ownership and control structure. The public control register cannot be relied on as the only source.
indicators: The declared structure cannot be reconciled with documents obtained from the customer
The customer is reluctant to explain who owns it
cards.why: Understanding the structure is a legal requirement, and enhanced measures are required wherever the risk is higher.
actions: Obtain and verify beneficial ownership information from the customer
Apply enhanced due diligence in higher risk situations
Keep the structure under review during the relationship
sources: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group, Guidance for the UK Financial Sector

cards.title: Reporting discrepancies in the control register
cards.summary: Where a regulated firm finds a material discrepancy between the control register and the beneficial ownership information it has obtained, it must report the discrepancy to the registrar.
indicators: The register names a different controller from the one the firm identified
The register shows no controller where the firm identified one
cards.why: Discrepancy reports are how the public register is corrected, and failing to report is a regulatory breach.
actions: File a discrepancy report with the registrar
Record the report in the customer file
sources: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017

cards.title: Suspicious activity reporting and tipping off
cards.summary: Where there is knowledge or suspicion of money laundering, a report must be made to the National Crime Agency through the nominated officer. The customer must not be told that a report has been made.
indicators: Findings that cannot be explained after reasonable enquiry
Customer explanations that conflict with the evidence
cards.why: Failure to disclose in the regulated sector and tipping off are criminal offences.
actions: Escalate to the nominated officer
Do not disclose the suspicion or the report to the customer
sources: Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, Part 7

cards.title: Limits of automated findings
cards.summary: Automated detection produces indicators of risk. It does not establish that an offence has taken place. Registry data contains errors, entity resolution can merge different people, and leak data is unverified.
indicators: A finding rests on a name only match
A finding rests on a single unresolved corporate link
The underlying filing is several years old
cards.why: Adverse action on an unverified finding can harm an innocent person and expose the firm to complaints and legal challenge.
actions: Have a trained reviewer confirm every finding before action
Record the evidence relied on and the decision reached
Feed confirmed and rejected findings back into tuning
sources: Joint Money Laundering Steering Group, Guidance for the UK Financial Sector
FATF, Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons (2023)

cards.title: Opaque partnership forms
cards.summary: Limited partnerships whose partners are offshore companies have been used in large laundering schemes because, historically, they disclosed little about who controlled them.
indicators: Partners are corporate entities registered in secrecy jurisdictions
The partnership has no evident business in the country of registration
The same corporate partners recur across many partnerships
cards.why: Partnership forms were for a long time outside the control register, which made them attractive as anonymous vehicles.
actions: Identify the natural persons behind each corporate partner
Check whether the partnership now reports its controllers
sources: HM Treasury and Home Office, National Risk Assessment of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (2020)
FATF and Egmont Group, Concealment of Beneficial Ownership (2018)
